transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hello, Mr Ferreira-Holt. I'm Dr Iyer from the first seizure clinic. And you're...?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Bethany, his wife. I was there when it happened.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: That's really helpful. Dominic, what do you remember?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Nothing, honestly. I was watching telly, and the next thing I knew there were paramedics in the living room.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: When was this?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Three weeks ago, on the Sunday night.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Bethany, can you tell me exactly what you saw?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: He went quiet, and then his left arm started jerking. Just the left arm, for a few seconds. Then he went stiff all over and started shaking all over.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How long did the shaking last?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: It felt like five minutes. But I looked at the clock when it started and when it stopped, and it was two minutes.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Two minutes. What did he look like?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: His lips went a bit blue. He bit his tongue, at the side, and he'd wet himself.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: And afterwards?

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: He was really confused for about twenty minutes. He didn't know where he was.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Dominic, had you been short of sleep, or drinking?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'd done four night shifts in a row. I'm a warehouse supervisor. I'd had maybe four hours' sleep.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any alcohol that day?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No. I have a few pints at the weekend, that's all.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any recreational drugs?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Have you ever had anything like this before? Any funny turns, jerks in the morning, or blank spells?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, never.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any head injuries, or meningitis as a child?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Anyone in the family with epilepsy?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Not that I know of.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any medicines? Allergies?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No and no.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Do you drive?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes, I drive to work.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'll come back to that. Let me examine you. Your neurological examination is completely normal today. Your CT scan in A&E was normal, and your blood tests were normal.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So what was it?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: This sounds like a seizure. Because it started with your left arm jerking, it may have started in one part of the brain, on the right side, before spreading. Lack of sleep can trigger seizures in people who are prone to them.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is it epilepsy?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Not necessarily. A single seizure isn't epilepsy. I'd like an MRI scan of your brain, using an epilepsy protocol, and an EEG, a recording of the brain's electrical activity.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay. Do I need tablets?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Not usually after a first seizure. We'll decide once we have the results.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Now, about driving. By law, you mustn't drive, and you need to tell the DVLA you've had a seizure. Usually you can't drive for six months after a first seizure, sometimes longer depending on the tests.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Six months? How will I get to work?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I know it's hard. Your employer may be able to help with shifts. Please don't drive in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: I'll drive him.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Some safety tips: have showers, not baths. Don't swim alone, and avoid heights. Try to keep a regular sleep pattern.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Bethany, if it happens again, put him on his side, time it, and call 999 if it lasts more than five minutes or he's injured.

transcript.speaker: Relative
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I'll see you in clinic with the results in about six weeks.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Thank you.

reference_note.history: No recollection of the event. Witnessed by wife: went quiet, then left arm jerking for a few seconds, followed by generalised stiffening and shaking lasting about 2 minutes (wife initially estimated 5 minutes, then confirmed 2 by the clock). Perioral cyanosis, lateral tongue bite, urinary incontinence. Post-ictal confusion for about 20 minutes. Preceded by sleep deprivation after four consecutive night shifts. No alcohol that day; a few pints at weekends. No drug use. No previous seizures, myoclonic jerks or absences. No head injury or CNS infection. No family history of epilepsy. Works as a warehouse supervisor. Drives.
reference_note.medications_allergies: No regular medications. No known drug allergies.
reference_note.examination: Neurological examination normal. CT head in ED normal. Bloods normal.
reference_note.impression: First generalised tonic-clonic seizure, possibly of focal onset (left arm, suggesting right hemisphere), provoked in part by sleep deprivation.
reference_note.plan: MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) and EEG. No antiseizure medication at present. Must not drive; patient to inform the DVLA (usually 6 months off driving after a first seizure). Safety advice: showers not baths, no swimming alone, avoid heights, regular sleep. Seizure first aid explained to wife. Clinic review with results in about 6 weeks.
reference_note.safety_netting: If a further seizure: recovery position, time it, call 999 if longer than 5 minutes or injured.
